questions.question: After a server action saves a new post, how do I make the posts list show it?
questions.searchedQuestion: After a server action saves a new post, how do I make the posts list show it in Next.js?

retrieved.headingPath: updateTag > Examples > Server Action with Read-Your-Own-Writes
Server Actions and Mutations > A single response carries data and UI
Mutating Data > Examples > Revalidate data
refresh > Examples
Mutating Data > Examples > Redirect after a mutation

questions.answer:
Call a cache-invalidation function inside the Server Action after the mutation. Which one depends on your setup:

## `revalidatePath`

Revalidate the path that shows the posts list [3]:

```ts
import { auth } from '@/lib/auth'
import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache'

export async function createPost(formData: FormData) {
  'use server'
  const session = await auth()
  if (!session?.user) {
    throw new Error('Unauthorized')
  }
  // Mutate data
  // ...

  revalidatePath('/posts')
}
```
[3]

`revalidateTag` is the other option the docs mention for this [3].

## `updateTag`

If your data is cached with tags, `updateTag` makes the new post immediately visible [1]:

```ts
'use server'

import { updateTag } from 'next/cache'
import { redirect } from 'next/navigation'

export async function createPost(formData: FormData) {
  const title = formData.get('title')
  const content = formData.get('content')

  const post = await db.post.create({
    data: { title, content },
  })

  updateTag('posts')
  updateTag(`post-${post.id}`)

  redirect(`/posts/${post.id}`)
}
```
[1]

The `'posts'` tag affects any page that displays a list of posts [1].

## `refresh`

Calling `refresh()` refetches the current route's RSC Payload [2][4]. It only works inside Server Actions and throws in a route handler [4].

## Redirecting afterward

If you redirect after the mutation, call the revalidation function first. `redirect` throws a control-flow exception, so code after it won't run [5].

```ts
revalidatePath('/posts')
redirect('/posts')
```
[5]

## What happens on the client

When the action calls `updateTag`, `revalidatePath`, `refresh`, or `redirect`, or mutates cookies, Next.js re-renders the current route in the same HTTP response as the action's return value. You don't need a follow-up fetch to see the updated UI [2].

questions.question: How do I expose an environment variable to code running in the browser?
questions.searchedQuestion: How do I expose an environment variable to code running in the browser?

retrieved.headingPath: How to use environment variables in Next.js > Bundling Environment Variables for the Browser
How to use environment variables in Next.js > Bundling Environment Variables for the Browser

How to use environment variables in Next.js > Bundling Environment Variables for the Browser > Runtime Environment Variables

questions.answer:
Prefix the variable name with `NEXT_PUBLIC_`. By default, environment variables are only available on the server. [4]

```txt
# .env
NEXT_PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_ID=abcdefghijk
```

At build time (`next build`), Next.js inlines the value into the JavaScript bundle sent to the browser, replacing references to `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_ID` with the hard-coded value. [1]

```js
setupAnalyticsService(process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_ID)
// becomes setupAnalyticsService('abcdefghijk') at build time
```

**Caveats:**

- **Values are frozen at build time.** After the build, the app no longer responds to changes in these variables. If you need runtime values in the browser, you have to set up your own API to provide them to the client. [1]
- **Dynamic lookups aren't inlined.** Use the full `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_...` form. Neither `process.env[varName]` nor `const env = process.env; env.NEXT_PUBLIC_...` will work. [2]

**Alternative:** you can add values to the bundle through the `env` key in `next.config.js`. These are always included in the bundle, and the `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix has no effect there. [3]

```js
// next.config.js
module.exports = {
  env: {
    customKey: 'my-value',
  },
}
```

Destructuring `process.env` variables won't work with this approach. [3]

questions.question: How do I set up Jest in a Next.js project?
questions.searchedQuestion: How do I set up Jest in a Next.js project?

retrieved.headingPath: How to set up Jest with Next.js > Quickstart
How to set up Jest with Next.js > Additional Resources
Testing Web Frameworks > Next.js
How to set up Jest with Next.js > Manual setup
How to set up Jest with Next.js > Manual setup

questions.answer:
There are two routes: a quickstart with the official example, or a manual setup.

## Quickstart

Use `create-next-app` with the `with-jest` example [1]:

```bash
npx create-next-app@latest --example with-jest with-jest-app
```

The docs also give pnpm, yarn and bun equivalents [1].

## Manual setup

**1. Install dev dependencies** [4]:

```bash
npm install -D jest jest-environment-jsdom @testing-library/react @testing-library/dom @testing-library/jest-dom ts-node @types/jest
```

**2. Generate a basic Jest config** [4]:

```bash
npm init jest@latest
```

This walks you through prompts and creates a `jest.config.ts|js` file [4].

**3. Update the config to use `next/jest`**, which provides the configuration Jest needs to work with Next.js [4][5]:

```ts
import type { Config } from 'jest'
import nextJest from 'next/jest.js'

const createJestConfig = nextJest({
  // Provide the path to your Next.js app to load next.config.js and .env files in your test environment
  dir: './',
})

// Add any custom config to be passed to Jest
const config: Config = {
  coverageProvider: 'v8',
  testEnvironment: 'jsdom',
  // Add more setup options before each test is run
  // setupFilesAfterEnv: ['<rootDir>/jest.setup.ts'],
}

// createJestConfig is exported this way to ensure that next/jest can load the Next.js config which is async
export default createJestConfig(config)
```
[5]

## What `next/jest` configures for you [5]

- `transform` using the Next.js Compiler
- Auto-mocking of stylesheets (`.css`, `.module.css`, and scss variants), image imports and `next/font`
- Loading `.env` (and variants) into `process.env`
- Ignoring `node_modules` for test resolving and transforms
- Ignoring `.next` for test resolving
- Loading `next.config.js` for flags that enable SWC transforms

To test environment variables directly, load them manually in a separate setup script or in your `jest.config.ts` [5].

questions.question: Are my .env files loaded when I run Jest tests in a Next.js app?
questions.searchedQuestion: Are .env files loaded when running Jest tests in a Next.js app?

retrieved.headingPath: How to use environment variables in Next.js > Test Environment Variables

questions.answer:
Yes, if you use `next/jest`. It loads `.env` files (and all variants) into `process.env` for you. [2][3] To make that work, pass the path to your Next.js app via the `dir` option so it can load `next.config.js` and `.env` files: [2]

```ts
import nextJest from 'next/jest.js'

const createJestConfig = nextJest({
  dir: './',
})
```

**Test environment specifics**
- When `NODE_ENV` is `test`, Next.js loads `.env.test`, not `.env.development` or `.env.production`. Testing tools usually set `NODE_ENV` for you. [1]
- `.env.local` is not loaded in the test environment, so tests produce the same results for everyone. [1]
- Commit `.env.test`, but not `.env.test.local`. [1]

**Testing environment variables directly**
If you need to test environment variables directly, load them manually in a separate setup script or in `jest.config.ts`. [2] You can use `loadEnvConfig` from `@next/env` to load them the same way Next.js does, for example in a Jest global setup file: [1]

```js
import { loadEnvConfig } from '@next/env'

export default async () => {
  const projectDir = process.cwd()
  loadEnvConfig(projectDir)
}
```

questions.question: What's the difference between toBe and toEqual?
questions.searchedQuestion: What's the difference between toBe and toEqual in Jest?

retrieved.headingPath: Expect > Matchers > .toBe(value)
Expect > Matchers > .toEqual(value)
Using Matchers > Common Matchers
Expect > Extend Utilities > expect.extend(matchers)
Expect > Matchers > .toStrictEqual(value)

questions.answer:
**`.toBe`** checks exact equality using `Object.is`. Use it for primitive values or to check referential identity of object instances. [1][3] Even when it fails on objects, it reports a deep comparison of values, though the check itself is by identity. [1]

**`.toEqual`** recursively compares all properties of objects or arrays ("deep" equality). It uses `Object.is` for primitive values. [2][3]

The difference shows up with two separate objects that have the same contents:

```js
const can1 = {flavor: 'grapefruit', ounces: 12};
const can2 = {flavor: 'grapefruit', ounces: 12};

expect(can1).toEqual(can2);     // passes: same properties
expect(can1).not.toBe(can2);    // passes: not the same instance
```
[2]

**Things to know about `.toEqual`:**
- It ignores object keys with `undefined` properties, `undefined` array items, array sparseness, and object type mismatch. Use `.toStrictEqual` if you need those checked. [2][5]
- It doesn't do a deep equality check on two errors. Only the `message` property is compared, so the docs recommend `.toThrow` for testing errors. [2]

**Thing to know about `.toBe`:**
- Don't use it with floating-point numbers, because `0.2 + 0.1` isn't strictly equal to `0.3`. Use `.toBeCloseTo` instead. [1]

**Rule of thumb:** use `toBe` for primitives and identity checks, and `toEqual` to check the value of an object. [1][3]

questions.answer:
Run Jest with the `--updateSnapshot` flag (or the single-character `-u`) to re-generate the snapshot artifacts:

```bash
jest --updateSnapshot
# or
jest -u
```

This re-generates snapshots for all failing snapshot tests [1]. Before you do, check that the change is intended. If any failures come from an unintentional bug, fix the bug first so you don't record snapshots of the buggy behavior [1][3].

**Update only some tests:** Add `--testNamePattern` to re-record only the tests that match the pattern [1].

**Update interactively:** In watch mode, Jest can step through failed snapshots one test at a time. You can review each failed output and choose to update that snapshot or skip to the next. Jest gives you a summary when you finish and returns to watch mode [2].

Commit the updated snapshot files along with your code changes [3].

questions.answer:
Use the `--testNamePattern` option (alias `-t`), which runs only tests whose name matches a regex. For example, to run tests related to authorization, such as `'GET /api/posts with auth'`:

```bash
jest -t=auth
```

[1]

You can also pass the name directly:

```bash
jest -t name-of-spec
```

[5]

The regex is matched against the full name, which combines the test name and all of its surrounding `describe` block names. [1] So the text can match either the `test` name or a `describe` name.

This differs from `jest <regexForTestFiles>`, which matches against file paths rather than test names. [2]

questions.answer:
Use Jest's `--coverage` CLI flag (alias `--collectCoverage`) to collect and report coverage in the output [1]:

```bash
jest --coverage
```

You can also enable it in your config with `collectCoverage` (default `false`). Coverage works by retrofitting all executed files with collection statements, so it can significantly slow your tests [3].

```js
// jest.config.js
const {defineConfig} = require('jest');

module.exports = defineConfig({
  collectCoverage: true,
});
```

The `collectCoverage` option itself is documented [3], but the exact `defineConfig` wrapper in this snippet is shown in the `coverageReporters` example [2].

**Useful related options**

- **Console summary:** The default `coverageReporters` are `["clover", "json", "lcov", "text"]`. If you override this option, add `"text"` or `"text-summary"` to see a summary in the console [2].
- **Hide fully covered files:** Use the tuple form, e.g. `['text', {skipFull: true}]` [2].
- **Output directory:** `--coverageDirectory=<path>` sets where coverage files are written [4].
- **Provider:** `--coverageProvider=<provider>` accepts `babel` (default) or `v8` [5].
- **Excluding lines:** The `babel` provider uses `/* istanbul ignore next */`, and `v8` uses `/* c8 ignore next */` [3].

questions.question: Whats the best way to render a really long scrolling list?
questions.searchedQuestion: What's the best way to render a really long scrolling list?

retrieved.headingPath: SectionList > Example
VirtualizedList > Example
VirtualizedList
ScrollView
Core Components and APIs > List Views

questions.answer:
Use a virtualized list component such as `FlatList` (or `SectionList` for sectioned data) instead of `ScrollView`.

- `ScrollView` renders all its child components at once, so a very long list means slow rendering and higher memory usage [4].
- `FlatList` renders items lazily, when they are about to appear, and removes items that scroll far off screen to save memory and processing time [4]. It also supports separators, multiple columns, and infinite scroll loading out of the box [4].
- `SectionList` is like `FlatList`, but for sectioned lists [5]. Both only render elements currently showing on screen, which makes them a performant choice for long lists [5].
- `VirtualizedList` is the base implementation for both. Use it only if you need more flexibility than `FlatList` provides, e.g. for immutable data instead of plain arrays [3].

**Caveats for these list components** [1][2]:

- Internal state isn't preserved when content scrolls out of the render window, so keep your data in the item data or an external store.
- They are `PureComponent`s, so they won't re-render if props are shallow-equal. Pass anything `renderItem` depends on as a prop (e.g. `extraData`) that changes identity on update.
- Content is rendered asynchronously offscreen, so scrolling faster than the fill rate can momentarily show blank content.
- The list uses each item's `key` prop by default, or you can provide a custom `keyExtractor`.

questions.question: How can I tell if the phone is in dark mode?
questions.searchedQuestion: How can I tell if the phone is in dark mode?

retrieved.headingPath: AccessibilityInfo > Reference > Methods > isDarkerSystemColorsEnabled() iOS

questions.answer:
Use the `Appearance` module or the `useColorScheme` hook. Both report the active color scheme.

## `Appearance.getColorScheme()`

```tsx
import {Appearance} from 'react-native';

const scheme = Appearance.getColorScheme(); // 'light' | 'dark' | null
const isDark = scheme === 'dark';
```

It returns `'light'`, `'dark'`, or `null` (which may happen if the native Appearance module isn't available). The value can change at runtime, either at the system level (e.g. a scheduled change at sunrise or sunset) or when overridden in the app via `setColorScheme()`. [5]

The color scheme maps to the user's Dark theme setting on Android 10 (API level 29) and higher, and to Dark Mode on iOS 13 and higher. [2]

## `useColorScheme` hook

The docs also point to the `useColorScheme` hook as the hook counterpart of `getColorScheme()`. [5] It returns the same values: `'light'`, `'dark'`, or `null`. [3]

## Not the same thing

`AccessibilityInfo.isDarkerSystemColorsEnabled()` (iOS) checks the "dark system colors" accessibility setting, not whether the device is in dark mode. [1]

The docs provided don't show a usage example for the hook, and they don't say how to subscribe to changes with `Appearance`.

questions.question: The keyboard covers my text input on iOS, how do I fix that?
questions.searchedQuestion: The keyboard covers my text input on iOS, how do I fix that?

🗑️ InputAccessoryView

questions.answer:
Wrap the interactive elements in a `KeyboardAvoidingView` so they stay accessible when the software keyboard appears. [1] The docs' example uses `behavior="padding"`:

```tsx
<KeyboardAvoidingView behavior="padding" style={styles.form}>
  <TextInput
    style={styles.input}
    value={email}
    onChangeText={text => setEmail(text)}
    ref={emailInput}
    placeholder="email@example.com"
    autoCapitalize="none"
    autoCorrect={false}
    keyboardType="email-address"
    returnKeyType="send"
    onSubmitEditing={submit}
    blurOnSubmit={true}
  />
  <View>
    <Button title="Sign Up" onPress={submit} />
    <Text style={styles.legal}>Some important legal fine print here</Text>
  </View>
</KeyboardAvoidingView>
```
[3][5]

In that demo, focusing the email input makes the Sign Up button and the text adjust their positions so they aren't hidden under the keyboard. [3][5]

**Alternative (iOS only, deprecated):** If you want the input anchored to the top of the keyboard, `InputAccessoryView` can create sticky text inputs: wrap a `TextInput` with it and don't set a `nativeID`. [4] However, this component is deprecated and will be removed in a future release. [2]

The docs provided don't cover other `KeyboardAvoidingView` props or `behavior` values beyond the `"padding"` example.

questions.answer:
Views stack vertically because React Native's Flexbox defaults differ from CSS on the web: `flexDirection` defaults to `column` instead of `row`. [1]

To place children side by side, set `flexDirection: 'row'` on the parent container. The Flex example in the docs uses `flexDirection: 'column'` and has a comment suggesting you try `"row"`. [3]

```jsx
<View style={{flex: 1, flexDirection: 'row'}}>
  <View style={{flex: 1, backgroundColor: 'red'}} />
  <View style={{flex: 2, backgroundColor: 'darkorange'}} />
  <View style={{flex: 3, backgroundColor: 'green'}} />
</View>
```

This snippet is adapted from the docs example, which uses `flexDirection: 'column'`. [3]

The docs say you'll normally combine `flexDirection`, `alignItems`, and `justifyContent` to get the layout you want. [1]

questions.question: What is Hermes and do I need to enable it?

questions.answer:
**What it is:** Hermes is an open-source JavaScript engine optimized for React Native. For many apps, it improves start-up time, lowers memory usage, and reduces app size compared to JavaScriptCore. [2] In release builds, JavaScript is compiled to bytecode ahead of time. That bytecode is loaded into memory on demand and doesn't need to be parsed like plain JavaScript. [3]

**Do you need to enable it?** No. Hermes is used by default in React Native, and no additional configuration is required. [2] It is the default engine for new React Native apps. [3] React Native also ships with a bundled version of Hermes, built for each React Native release so it's compatible with the version you're using. [1] The bundled Hermes compiler (`hermesc`) is used by default as well, so you generally don't need to customize its path. [4]

**Opting out:** You can still disable Hermes. [1] React Native supports JavaScriptCore as an alternative engine, and the instructions for opting out are in the community repository. [5]

questions.question: How do I generate a signed release build for the Google Play Store?
questions.searchedQuestion: How do I generate a signed release build for the Google Play Store?

retrieved.headingPath: Publishing to Google Play Store > Adding signing config to your app's Gradle config
Publishing to Google Play Store > Generating the release AAB
Running On Device > Building your app for production

Publishing to Google Play Store

questions.answer:
Generating a signed release build has two parts in the docs: set up the signing config, then build the AAB. The docs provided don't cover creating the upload key or the `gradle.properties` entries, so see the note at the end.

## 1. Add the signing config

Release builds must be signed with an upload key. Edit `android/app/build.gradle` and add the signing config [1]:

```groovy
...
android {
    ...
    defaultConfig { ... }
    signingConfigs {
        release {
            if (project.hasProperty('MYAPP_UPLOAD_STORE_FILE')) {
                storeFile file(MYAPP_UPLOAD_STORE_FILE)
                storePassword MYAPP_UPLOAD_STORE_PASSWORD
                keyAlias MYAPP_UPLOAD_KEY_ALIAS
                keyPassword MYAPP_UPLOAD_KEY_PASSWORD
            }
        }
    }
    buildTypes {
        release {
            ...
            signingConfig signingConfigs.release
        }
    }
}
...
```

## 2. Generate the release AAB

```shell
npx react-native build-android --mode=release
```

This uses Gradle's `bundleRelease` to bundle the JavaScript into the AAB (Android App Bundle) [2]. The output is at `android/app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab`, ready to upload to Google Play [2].

Things to watch for:
- Make sure `gradle.properties` does not include `org.gradle.configureondemand=true`, since it makes the release build skip bundling JS and assets [2].
- Google Play must have App Signing by Google Play configured in the Play Console to accept the AAB format [2].

## 3. Test the release build (recommended)

Uninstall any previous version of the app, then run [4]:

```shell
npm run android -- --mode="release"
```

or

```shell
yarn android --mode release
```

`--mode release` only works if signing is set up as above [4].

## Not covered

The provided docs don't show how to generate the upload key or where to define the `MYAPP_UPLOAD_*` properties used in the Gradle config.

If you use Expo, the docs point to Expo's guide for [Deploying to App Stores](https://docs.expo.dev/distribution/app-stores/) [5].

questions.question: How do I make a value that's derived from other signals?
questions.searchedQuestion: How do I make a value that's derived from other signals?

retrieved.headingPath: Dependent state with linkedSignal > Accounting for previous state
Angular Signals > What are signals? > Computed signals
Signals > Computed expressions
Angular Signals > What are signals? > Computed signals
Signal write in a disallowed context > Writing to signals is not allowed in a computed

questions.answer:
Use a `computed` signal. It derives its value from other signals and is read-only. [2][3]

```typescript
import {signal, computed} from '@angular/core';

const count = signal(0);
const doubleCount = computed(() => count() * 2);
```

[2]

Key behaviors:

- **Automatic updates:** When any signal read inside the derivation changes, the computed value updates. [3]

```typescript
const firstName = signal('Morgan');
const firstNameCapitalized = computed(() => firstName().toUpperCase());
console.log(firstNameCapitalized()); // MORGAN

firstName.set('Jaime');
console.log(firstNameCapitalized()); // JAIME
```

[3]

- **Lazy and memoized:** The derivation doesn't run until the first read, and the result is cached until a dependency changes. This makes it safe to do expensive work such as filtering arrays. [2]
- **Read-only:** Calling `set` on a computed signal is a compilation error. [2][3]
- **Dynamic dependencies:** Only signals actually read during the derivation are tracked. [2]
- **No side effects:** Don't write to other signals inside a `computed`. If a value only depends on other signals, make it a `computed` rather than storing it in a separate signal. [5]

```typescript
count = signal(1);
total = computed(() => this.count() * 2);
```

[5]

If the derived value also needs to be writable, use `linkedSignal`. [1][5] It accepts a `source` and a `computation`, and the computation can use the `previous` object to decide the new value. [1]

Use an effect. The docs list "keeping data in sync with different kinds of storage: `window.localStorage`, session storage, cookies, etc." as an appropriate use case, along with logging signal values and custom DOM behavior [3]. Effects are best for syncing signal state to imperative, non-signal APIs [3].

Some caveats from the docs:
- Effects should be the last API you reach for. Prefer `computed()` for derived values and `linkedSignal()` for values that can be both derived and manually set [3].
- Don't use effects to propagate state changes from one signal to another. This can cause `ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenChecked` errors, infinite circular updates, or unnecessary change detection cycles [3].

questions.answer:
Yes, in Angular. Use a `@defer` block with the `viewport` trigger, which loads the deferred content when the specified content enters the viewport [3]. `@defer` splits the code for components, directives, and pipes inside the block into a separate JavaScript file that loads only when necessary [5].

You can also add a prefetch trigger so the JavaScript loads before the content is shown. It uses the `prefetch` keyword, separated from the main trigger by a semicolon [4]. The docs only show prefetch examples with `on interaction; prefetch on idle`, not with `viewport`.

**Caveat:** Avoid deferring components that are visible in the viewport on initial load, since this can increase cumulative layout shift (CLS). If you must, avoid `immediate`, `timer`, `viewport`, and custom `when` triggers that load content during the initial page render [1].

**Not covered by the docs provided:** The context doesn't include a complete `viewport` trigger example or its syntax details (such as specifying a reference element). It also doesn't describe a scroll-into-view mechanism for React Native or Next.js. For React Native, the docs only cover deferring a component's code until its first render with React's `lazy` [2], not until it scrolls into view.

questions.question: How do I run my app without zone.js?
questions.searchedQuestion: How do I run my Angular app without zone.js?

retrieved.headingPath: Angular without ZoneJS (Zoneless) > Removing ZoneJS
Angular without ZoneJS (Zoneless) > Enabling Zoneless in an application

Version compatibility > Polyfills for non-CLI users

questions.answer:
Which steps you need depends on your Angular version.

## 1. Enable zoneless change detection

**Angular v21+:** Zoneless is the default, so there's nothing to enable. Just make sure `provideZoneChangeDetection` isn't used anywhere to override the default. [2]

**Angular v20:** Add `provideZonelessChangeDetection()` at bootstrap [2]:

```ts
bootstrapApplication(MyApp, {providers: [provideZonelessChangeDetection()]});
```

Or with NgModule:

```ts
platformBrowser().bootstrapModule(AppModule);

@NgModule({
  providers: [provideZonelessChangeDetection()],
})
export class AppModule {}
```
[2]

## 2. Remove ZoneJS from the build

- In `angular.json`, remove `zone.js` and `zone.js/testing` from the `polyfills` option in both the `build` and `test` targets. [1]
- If you use an explicit `polyfills.ts`, remove `import 'zone.js';` and `import 'zone.js/testing';`. [1]

## 3. Uninstall the package

```shell
npm uninstall zone.js
```
[1]

## 4. Make your code zoneless-compatible

- Remove uses of `NgZone.onMicrotaskEmpty`, `NgZone.onUnstable`, and `NgZone.onStable`, since they never emit in zoneless apps. `NgZone.isStable` is always `true`, so don't use it as a condition. [4]
- Replace them with `afterNextRender` (wait for a single change detection) or `afterEveryRender` (a condition that may span several rounds). For waiting on specific DOM state, `MutationObserver` can be used. [4]
- You don't need to remove `NgZone.run` or `NgZone.runOutsideAngular`. They're compatible with zoneless, and removing them can cause performance regressions for libraries used in apps that still rely on ZoneJS. [4]
